section: The static-budget trap, and the flexible-budget fix
text:
The static-budget trap, and the flexible-budget fix
What the stand just built has names. The original plan, priced for a volume that didn’t happen, is the static budget — compare actuals straight against it and you blame people for the volume (the owner’s mistake). The same plan re-stated at actual volume — prices and unit costs stay at budget; only the volume moves — is the flexible budget; it splits every miss into “we sold fewer” (the sales-volume variance, valued at budgeted contribution per unit) and “per unit, we did better or worse” (the flexible-budget variance).
Now the same month-end, four zeros longer. Tesla set Q4 2024 targets. The headline: it missed — it delivered fewer cars than planned, and the quarter’s operating profit landed below budget. The board’s question: was that the market (we sold fewer cars, at lower revenue per car) or the factory (our costs)? (The figures below are simulated — built on Tesla’s real Q4 2024 as a base — so treat this as an illustrative case.)

v = pd.read_csv('../../data/simulated/variance_analysis_q4.csv').set_index('item')
def ba(item): return v.loc[item, 'budget'], v.loc[item, 'actual']

# One volume = cars. We treat cars MADE = cars SOLD (the standard intro simplification),
# so a single volume drives both revenue and cost — no inventory to worry about.
bV, aV   = ba('deliveries')
bP, aP   = ba('revenue_per_car_delivered')
bM, aM   = ba('direct_materials_per_unit')
bL, aL   = ba('direct_labor_per_unit')
bO, aO   = ba('variable_overhead_per_unit')
bF, aF   = [x*1e6 for x in ba('fixed_costs_millions')]   # to $

bVC, aVC = bM+bL+bO, aM+aL+aO      # budget / actual variable cost per car
print(f"Cars (budget vs actual):  {bV:,.0f}  vs  {aV:,.0f}   ({aV-bV:+,.0f})")
print(f"Revenue / car delivered*: ${bP:,.0f}  vs  ${aP:,.0f}")
print(f"Variable cost / car:      ${bVC:,.0f}  vs  ${aVC:,.0f}   "
      f"(materials {aM-bM:+,.0f}, labour {aL-bL:+,.0f}, var-OH {aO-bO:+,.0f})")
print(f"Fixed cost ($m):          {bF/1e6:,.0f}  vs  {aF/1e6:,.0f}")

Cars (budget vs actual):  500,000  vs  495,570   (-4,430)
Revenue / car delivered*: $52,000  vs  $51,900
Variable cost / car:      $28,500  vs  $28,800   (materials +500, labour -300, var-OH +100)
Fixed cost ($m):          9,750  vs  9,800


*Revenue per car delivered = total revenue spread over cars — it includes energy, services & credits, so it sits above the ~$43k Model Y sticker. Session 2’s proxy, not an “ASP”.






NoteOne pot of fixed costs — and a reality check



The $9,750m fixed pot is all of Tesla’s fixed costs — fixed production overhead plus R&D plus SG&A — rolled into one line. That makes the bottom line below (approximately) quarterly operating profit, and the magnitude survives a reality check: Tesla’s real Q4 2024 operating profit landed at ≈$1.6bn, and ours will too. If you’re wondering why this pot is so much bigger than Session 2’s regression intercept: that regression estimated the fixed part of cost of revenues only (≈$4.3bn a quarter); today’s pot also carries R&D and SG&A.








NoteIn Excel (same answers, live formulas)





Download ac101-s5-variance.xlsx: change any budget or actual figure and watch the static → flexible → actual profit, the volume variance, and every line variance update.



The smoothie move at Tesla’s scale — the same plan re-stated at the volume actually hit:

def profit(V, P, VC, F): return (P - VC) * V - F           # operating profit, $
static = profit(bV, bP, bVC, bF)                            # plan
flex   = profit(aV, bP, bVC, bF)                            # plan re-flexed to actual volume
actual = profit(aV, aP, aVC, aF)                            # reality

print(f"{'':22}{'Static budget':>15}{'Flexible budget':>17}{'Actual':>13}")
print(f"{'':22}{'(plan, 500k)':>15}{'(actual vol)':>17}{'':>13}")
print("-"*67)
print(f"{'Cars sold':22}{bV:>15,.0f}{aV:>17,.0f}{aV:>13,.0f}")
print(f"{'Operating profit $m':22}{static/1e6:>15,.0f}{flex/1e6:>17,.0f}{actual/1e6:>13,.0f}")
print("-"*67)
vol_var  = flex - static       # sales-volume variance
flex_var = actual - flex       # flexible-budget (price/efficiency) variance
print(f"\n  Sales-VOLUME variance (static→flexible):  ${vol_var/1e6:>+8,.0f}m  "
      f"{'F' if vol_var>=0 else 'U'}   ← we sold fewer cars")
print(f"  Flexible-budget variance (flexible→actual): ${flex_var/1e6:>+8,.0f}m  "
      f"{'F' if flex_var>=0 else 'U'}   ← per-car price & costs")
print(f"  TOTAL profit variance:                     ${(actual-static)/1e6:>+8,.0f}m  "
      f"{'F' if actual>=static else 'U'}")

                        Static budget  Flexible budget       Actual
                         (plan, 500k)     (actual vol)             
-------------------------------------------------------------------
Cars sold                     500,000          495,570      495,570
Operating profit $m             2,000            1,896        1,648
-------------------------------------------------------------------

  Sales-VOLUME variance (static→flexible):  $    -104m  U   ← we sold fewer cars
  Flexible-budget variance (flexible→actual): $    -248m  U   ← per-car price & costs
  TOTAL profit variance:                     $    -352m  U


On paper: the volume variance = cars short × budgeted contribution per car = −4,430 × $23,500 ($52,000 − $28,500) ≈ −$104m U — this is the contribution basis (recall contribution margin, Session 2), and it is the basis the exam uses.






ImportantMisconception check




Don’t compare actual to the original budget directly — flex to actual volume first, or you punish the factory for the sales team’s volume.
Sign of a variance: for revenue, actual > budget is Favourable; for a cost, actual > budget is Unfavourable (you spent more). Keep them straight.

section: Inside a line variance — price vs quantity (standard costing)
text:
Inside a line variance — price vs quantity (standard costing)
The table says materials cost an extra $248m — but why? Did the factory pay more per input, or use more inputs per car? Those have different owners (purchasing vs the production line), so lumping them together hides exactly what a manager needs to know.
The tool is a standard cost card — the heart of standard costing. For each input you set, in advance, a standard price (for labour, a standard rate) and a standard quantity per unit of output. Here is ours (simulated, like the rest of today’s figures):



Input
Standard card
= per car




Direct materials
400 units @ $45
$18,000


Direct labour
60 hours @ $75
$4,500



This quarter the factory actually used 370 units @ $50 of materials per car. To split the line, move one thing at a time — build the middle step: start at the card, 400 × $45 = $18,000; change the quantity first, at standard price, 370 × $45 = $16,650 (using 30 fewer units saved 30 × $45 = $1,350 F); then change the price on the units actually used, 370 × $50 = $18,500 (paying $5 more on each of 370 units cost $1,850 U). The two named formulas are a record of that walk:

Price variance = (Std price − Act price) × Act qty = ($45 − $50) × 370 = −$1,850 U per car
Quantity variance = (Std qty − Act qty) × Std price = (400 − 370) × $45 = +$1,350 F per car

Net: −$500 U per car — exactly the materials overrun ($18,000 → $18,500). Multiply by the cars actually built and the split reconciles with the table above:

# Simulated standard cost card (materials): 400 units @ $45 = $18,000 per car
sp, ap, sq, aq = 45, 50, 400, 370            # std/act price, std/act qty per car
price_var = (sp - ap) * aq * aV / 1e6        # (Std price - Act price) x Act qty
qty_var   = (sq - aq) * sp * aV / 1e6        # (Std qty - Act qty)   x Std price
print(f"Materials PRICE variance:    {price_var:>+8,.1f} $m  {'F' if price_var>=0 else 'U'}   (paid $50, not $45)")
print(f"Materials QUANTITY variance: {qty_var:>+8,.1f} $m  {'F' if qty_var>=0 else 'U'}   (used 370 units, not 400)")
print(f"Sum:                         {price_var+qty_var:>+8,.1f} $m  = the materials line above")

Materials PRICE variance:      -916.8 $m  U   (paid $50, not $45)
Materials QUANTITY variance:   +669.0 $m  F   (used 370 units, not 400)
Sum:                           -247.8 $m  = the materials line above


So the flexed materials line was hiding a much bigger story: a price hit of −$917m (input prices spiked), nearly three-quarters offset by a genuine quantity win of +$669m (less material per car). Same total, completely different management conversation.
Scenario note: the input-price spike is simulated. Lithium really did spike roughly tenfold in 2022 — but through 2024 it was falling to multi-year lows, so treat this quarter’s spike as a what-if, not history.
Terminology, once: the quantity side also goes by usage or efficiency variance — same formula, three names. For labour, convention says rate (the price side) and efficiency (the quantity side). And at the total level the standard quantity allowed is flexed to actual output — actual cars × standard quantity per car — the flexible-budget principle all over again.






NoteYour turn — split the labour line



The card says 60 hours @ $75; the factory actually used 50 hours @ $84 per car. Calculator only: compute the labour rate and efficiency variances per car (F/U each), and check they net to +$300 F per car — the +$149m labour line.








NoteReveal





Rate = ($75 − $84) × 50 = −$450 U; efficiency = (60 − 50) × $75 = +$750 F; net +$300 F per car. Scaled by 495,570 cars: rate −$223.0m U, efficiency +$371.7m F, net +$148.7m F. The table’s “labour win” is really a big efficiency gain (automation, learning) partly eaten by pricier hours (overtime, skilled technicians).

title: Session 5 — Variance Analysis
section: Management by exception — don’t chase noise
text:
Management by exception — don’t chase noise






TipDefine it well



Management by exception: investigate only the variances that are big and controllable — ignore the small and the uncontrollable. Spending the CFO’s attention on a $50m fixed-cost wobble while a $248m materials hit and a $104m volume shortfall sit there is exactly backwards.


For this quarter, the exceptions worth a manager’s time:

Materials (−$248m): the largest controllable-ish hit — a hedging failure, or a genuine world-price move? Procurement review.
The volume shortfall: was it demand (fewer buyers at the price) or supply (couldn’t build enough)? That decides whether it’s the sales team’s or the plant’s issue.
Labour (+$149m): a favourable exception — find out what worked and spread it.

The rest (revenue per car, overhead, fixed) is small — below the materiality line, so whoever owns it, it waits. An exception is big and controllable; a small wobble isn’t worth the CFO’s attention.
One caveat, though: a small net can still hide large offsetting components with different owners — so glance inside the biggest-net lines before dismissing them. The case’s E6 (a one-off restructuring charge buried inside the fixed line) and E7 ▸ (a −$545m rate hit against a +$496m efficiency win inside variable overhead) are the worked illustrations of exactly this.






NoteYour turn — the variance memo



You’re the analyst; the CFO wants three bullets on the quarter’s $352m profit miss:

What happened — the two or three variances that actually drove the miss (numbers and F/U).
What to investigate — which variances deserve management attention, and who owns each.
One recommendation for next quarter.

Draft it solo, then swap with a neighbour: does their memo chase anything uncontrollable — or noise?








Note▸ Two caveats before you trust any variance






Was the budget real? Musk’s public targets are famously aspirational (the “20 million cars by 2030” goal was quietly dropped in 2024). A “favourable” variance against a soft budget isn’t performance; an “unfavourable” one against a moon-shot isn’t failure. Variances are only as good as the budget.
Variances can be gamed. Tie a bonus to hitting a profit number and people find levers — delaying maintenance, padding budgets, or (recall Session 3) overproducing to park fixed cost in inventory. That’s the bridge to Part 2, where we design bonuses that don’t reward it.

Both caveats have hard evidence behind them: Bouwens & Kroos (2011, JAE) studied store managers at a retail chain where beating this year’s sales target ratchets next year’s target up. Managers comfortably ahead of target by Q3 measurably eased off in Q4 — slowing down protected them from a tougher target next year. The budget wasn’t just measuring behaviour; it was driving it.





Stylised illustration of Bouwens & Kroos (2011): managers who have already met the annual target ease off in Q4, because beating it further only ratchets next year’s target. (Illustrative pattern, not the paper’s data.)

title: Session 5 — Variance Analysis
text:
Key takeaways






NoteKey takeaways




Flex the budget to actual volume first — it separates “we sold fewer” (volume, priced at budgeted contribution per unit: the contribution basis) from “per car we did better/worse” (price & efficiency).
Variances split into sales volume, revenue per car, materials, labour, overhead and fixed — each owned by someone; inside an input line, the standard cost card splits further into price (rate) × quantity (efficiency).
Every split is one move: build the middle step and change one thing at a time — the flexible budget between plan and reality, the standard-price column between the card and the invoice. Forget a formula → rebuild the walk.
Controllability: judge managers only on what they control.
Management by exception: chase the big, controllable variances (here: materials and the volume shortfall); reinforce favourable ones (labour); ignore the noise — but glance inside big nets.
A variance is only as trustworthy as the budget behind it — and punitive use invites gaming.

ImportantThe message



A cost becomes an expense only when it earns its revenue. And that is why deliveries — cars sold — drive COGS while production doesn’t (R² 0.84 vs 0.15 in Session 2): the regression agreed with the accounting.

title: Session 3 — Cost Allocation & ABC
section: R² — the share of the misses the line removes
text:
R² — the share of the misses the line removes
With no line, your best guess for any month’s cost is the average. R² asks how much better the line does:

from scipy import stats

demo = pd.read_csv('../../data/teaching/monthly_cost_demo.csv')
d_s, d_i, d_r, d_p, d_se = stats.linregress(demo['units'], demo['total_cost'])
sst = ((demo['total_cost'] - demo['total_cost'].mean())**2).sum()   # misses around the average
sse = ((demo['total_cost'] - (d_i + d_s*demo['units']))**2).sum()   # misses around the line

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4), sharey=True)
ybar = demo['total_cost'].mean()
pred = d_i + d_s*demo['units']
a1.scatter(demo['units'], demo['total_cost'], s=55, color=BLUE, alpha=.75, edgecolors='black', zorder=5)
a1.axhline(ybar, color='0.35', lw=2)
a1.vlines(demo['units'], ybar, demo['total_cost'], color=TESLA_RED, ls=':', lw=1.8)
a1.set_title('No line: guess with the average'); a1.set_xlabel('Units'); a1.set_ylabel('Total cost (£)')
a2.scatter(demo['units'], demo['total_cost'], s=55, color=BLUE, alpha=.75, edgecolors='black', zorder=5)
xs = np.linspace(demo['units'].min(), demo['units'].max(), 40)
a2.plot(xs, d_i + d_s*xs, color='navy', lw=2)
a2.vlines(demo['units'], pred, demo['total_cost'], color=TESLA_RED, ls=':', lw=1.8)
a2.set_title('With the line: the misses shrink'); a2.set_xlabel('Units')
for a_ in (a1, a2): a_.grid(True, alpha=.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 1: Left: guessing every month with the average — the dotted gaps are the misses. Right: guessing with the regression line — the misses shrink. R² is the share of the (squared) misses the line removes.






print(f"Squared misses around the average : {sst:,.0f}")
print(f"Squared misses around the line    : {sse:,.0f}")
print(f"Share the line removes            : 1 − {sse/sst:.3f} = {1 - sse/sst:.3f}")

Squared misses around the average : 4,926,916,667
Squared misses around the line    : 781,014,208
Share the line removes            : 1 − 0.159 = 0.841


That is R². R² = 0.841 means the line removes 84% of the variation the average leaves behind. Formally: \(R^2 = 1 - \sum(Y-\hat{Y})^2 / \sum(Y-\bar{Y})^2\). R² tells you how much to lean on the line — never that the line is right (recall B6: total revenue fitted COGS at R² = 0.963 and was still the wrong driver).

title: Session 3 — Cost Allocation & ABC
text:
The p-value — the luck question
Session 2’s slope said $31,951 per car, with p = 0.0013. The p-value answers one worry: with only 8 quarters, couldn’t a slope that size appear by pure luck — even if deliveries had nothing to do with COGS? Break the link on purpose and see:

tq = pd.read_csv('../../data/raw/tesla_quarterly.csv')
tq = tq[tq['year'].isin([2023, 2024])].copy()
dels = tq['deliveries'].values.astype(float)
cogs = tq['cogs_millions'].values.astype(float)
ts, ti, tr, tp_, tse = stats.linregress(dels, cogs)

rng = np.random.default_rng(101)                      # seeded — rerun and you get the same picture
shuffle_slopes = np.array([stats.linregress(dels, rng.permutation(cogs)).slope
                           for _ in range(2_000)]) * 1e6
n_reached = int((np.abs(shuffle_slopes) >= abs(ts*1e6)).sum())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.hist(shuffle_slopes, bins=45, color=BLUE, alpha=.75, edgecolor='white')
ax.axvline(ts*1e6, color=TESLA_RED, lw=2.5)
ax.annotate(f'our slope: ${ts*1e6:,.0f}', xy=(ts*1e6, 45), xytext=(ts*1e6 - 24_000, 72),
            fontsize=10, color=TESLA_RED, fontweight='bold',
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=TESLA_RED))
ax.set_xlabel('Slope luck produced ($ per car)'); ax.set_ylabel('Shuffles')
ax.set_title('What "statistically significant" looks like')
ax.grid(True, alpha=.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"Shuffles (out of 2,000) that reached the real slope: {n_reached}")







Figure 2: Shuffle the eight COGS numbers across the quarters (destroying any real link), refit the line, repeat 2,000 times. The blue mound is what luck alone produces; the red line is the real slope.





Shuffles (out of 2,000) that reached the real slope: 0


In 2,000 shuffles, luck never once reached our slope. The regression’s p = 0.0013 asks exactly this question with a formula instead of shuffling: if the true slope were zero, chance would produce one this strong about once in 750 tries. That is all statistically significant means — too strong to be luck (convention: p < 0.05). It is not the accuracy of the estimate, and not the probability the answer is right.






TipDefine it well



Statistically significant — too strong to be luck (small p). Says nothing about size. Economically significant — big enough to change a decision. Says nothing about certainty.
Two illustrations: a paint-shop electricity slope of $9 per car with p = 0.001 is certainly real and utterly irrelevant next to $31,951 of variable cost (statistically yes, economically no). A supplier-rebate effect of −$2,100 per car with p = 0.31 would matter enormously if real, but eight quarters can’t tell (economically yes, statistically not yet — get more data before acting). Act on numbers that are both.

title: Session 3 — Cost Allocation & ABC
section: Use the output — classify cost accounts by their p-values
text:
Use the output — classify cost accounts by their p-values
Regression output is for three things: the split feeds decisions (CVP, forecasts, the case); R² says how far to trust the line; and the p-values classify cost behaviour, account by account — this is how a finance team actually splits a ledger:

# SIMULATED quarterly cost accounts (labelled): built on the REAL 2023–24
# deliveries, plausible magnitudes, seed fixed — Tesla does not publish this detail.
rng2 = np.random.default_rng(19)
acct = pd.DataFrame({
    'Factory security & insurance': 44 + rng2.normal(0, 2.2, 8),
    'Battery cells & materials':    0.0209 * dels + rng2.normal(0, 55, 8),
    'Plant power & maintenance':    220 + 0.00025 * dels + rng2.normal(0, 5, 8),
})
def fit_account(y):
    res = stats.linregress(dels, y)
    t_int = res.intercept / res.intercept_stderr
    p_int = 2 * (1 - stats.t.cdf(abs(t_int), len(dels) - 2))
    return res.intercept, p_int, res.slope*1e6, res.pvalue, res.rvalue**2

print(f"{'ACCOUNT':<34}{'Intercept (p)':>18}{'Slope/car (p)':>20}{'R²':>8}")
print("-" * 80)
for name in acct:
    a0, pa, b1, pb, r2 = fit_account(acct[name])
    pa_s = f"{pa:.3f}" if pa >= 0.001 else "<0.001"
    pb_s = f"{pb:.3f}" if pb >= 0.001 else "<0.001"
    print(f"{name:<34}{f'${a0:,.0f}m ({pa_s})':>18}{f'${b1:,.0f} ({pb_s})':>20}{r2:>8.2f}")

ACCOUNT                                Intercept (p)       Slope/car (p)      R²
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Factory security & insurance            $50m (0.002)        $-13 (0.537)    0.07
Battery cells & materials             $-163m (0.518)    $21,313 (<0.001)    1.00
Plant power & maintenance             $213m (<0.001)        $263 (0.002)    0.83








NoteYour turn (then check)



For each account: fixed, variable or mixed? Use only the p-values — which pieces of each line are real? ▸ One intercept is negative. Why is that not alarming here?








NoteReveal






Factory security & insurance → FIXED. The intercept is real (p = 0.002); the slope is noise (−$13, p = 0.54).
Battery cells & materials → VARIABLE. The slope is emphatically real ($21,313/car, p < 0.001); the intercept is noise (p = 0.52).
Plant power & maintenance → MIXED. Both pieces are real ($213m base; $263/car) — a genuine \(a + bX\).
▸ The −$163m “fixed cost” is the same tell as B6’s −$573m: an impossible number estimated from noise — its p-value (0.52) says exactly that. Read the p-value before you read the coefficient.

The rule: a coefficient without a credible p-value isn’t a number — it’s a guess wearing one.

title: Session 3 — Cost Allocation & ABC
text:
Break-even, derived — not just drawn
Start from what profit is, using Session 2’s cost function:
\[\pi \;=\; \underbrace{P \cdot Q}_{\text{revenue}} - \underbrace{(FC + VC \cdot Q)}_{\text{total cost}} \;=\; (P - VC)\cdot Q - FC \;=\; \text{CM}\cdot Q - FC\]
Set \(\pi = 0\) for break-even: \(Q^{*} = FC/\text{CM}\). Want a target profit \(\pi^{*}\)? \(Q = (FC + \pi^{*})/\text{CM}\) — the pile just grows by the target. Sanity check on Tesla: $4,295m ÷ $22,648 ≈ 190,000 cars a quarter — Session 2’s number, now proved rather than pictured.

rev24 = tq.loc[tq['year'] == 2024, 'revenue_millions'].sum()
del24 = tq.loc[tq['year'] == 2024, 'deliveries'].sum()
rev_per_car = rev24 * 1e6 / del24
cm_unit  = rev_per_car - ts*1e6
fixed_q  = ti
be_units = fixed_q*1e6 / cm_unit
actual_q = del24 / 4

qv = np.linspace(0, actual_q*1.25, 200)
pi_m = (cm_unit*qv - fixed_q*1e6) / 1e6
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.plot(qv/1000, pi_m, color='navy', lw=2.5)
ax.axhline(0, color='0.4', lw=1.2)
ax.fill_between(qv/1000, pi_m, 0, where=(pi_m < 0), color=TESLA_RED, alpha=.12)
ax.fill_between(qv/1000, pi_m, 0, where=(pi_m >= 0), color='seagreen', alpha=.12)
ax.scatter([0], [-fixed_q], s=55, color=TESLA_RED, zorder=5)
ax.axvline(be_units/1000, color='black', ls=':', alpha=.6)
ax.annotate(f'π = 0 at Q* ≈ {be_units/1000:.0f}k', xy=(be_units/1000, 0),
            xytext=(be_units/1000 + 18, -2600), fontsize=10)
ax.axvline(actual_q/1000, color='navy', ls='--', alpha=.6)
ax.annotate(f'actual ≈ {actual_q/1000:.0f}k', xy=(actual_q/1000, 0),
            xytext=(actual_q/1000 + 8, 1200), fontsize=10, color='navy')
ax.set_xlabel('Deliveries per quarter (000s)'); ax.set_ylabel('Quarterly profit, $m (COGS basis)')
ax.grid(True, alpha=.3)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 3: π = CM·Q − FC is a straight line in Q: it starts at −FC (sell nothing, lose the whole pile), climbs by CM per car, and crosses zero at Q*.

The simplest rule: split by volume (traditional allocation)
The most common method spreads overhead by production volume — one rate per car (accountants call it a plant-wide rate), on the logic “more cars, more cost.”

title: Session 3 — Cost Allocation & ABC
section: Activity-based costing (ABC): charge each cost to what drives it
text:
Activity-based costing (ABC): charge each cost to what drives it
ABC splits overhead into cost pools, each with its own cost driver — the thing that actually causes that cost — then charges each model for the drivers it uses.






NoteIn Excel (same answer, no code)





Download ac101-s3-cost-allocation.xlsx: the Calc sheet builds the blended rate and the five ABC pool rates with SUMPRODUCT, then allocates to each model — all live formulas. Change Cybertruck’s assembly hours on the Products sheet and watch its cost and margin move.



One rate by hand before any code. The assembly pool costs $2,400 m a year, and the five models together use 14.56 m assembly hours (each model’s hours per car × its volume, summed). So the rate is $2,400 m ÷ 14.56 m hours ≈ $165 per assembly hour — and a Cybertruck, at 25 hours, picks up 25 × $165 ≈ $4,100 of assembly overhead alone. That’s the whole ABC mechanic.






NoteYour turn — one ABC rate by hand



Now you: the battery systems pool costs $3,200 m a year, and the five models together use 87.67 m kWh of battery capacity. What’s the rate per kWh? Calculator only — exactly how the exam will ask it.








NoteReveal





$3,200 m ÷ 87.67 m kWh ≈ $36.50 per kWh. Check it against the ACTIVITY RATES table the next cell prints.




# Total activity for each driver
prod['tot_assembly'] = prod['annual_volume_fremont'] * prod['assembly_hours_per_unit']
prod['tot_kwh']      = prod['annual_volume_fremont'] * prod['kwh_capacity']
prod['tot_tests']    = prod['annual_volume_fremont'] * prod['test_cycles_per_unit']
driver_tot = {'assembly_hours': prod['tot_assembly'].sum(),
              'kwh_capacity':   prod['tot_kwh'].sum(),
              'test_cycles':    prod['tot_tests'].sum(),
              'shipments':      prod['annual_volume_fremont'].sum(),
              'facility_floor': prod['annual_volume_fremont'].sum()}

# Rate for each pool = pool cost / total driver volume
rate_of = {p['cost_pool']: p['annual_cost_millions']*1e6 / driver_tot[p['cost_driver']]
           for _, p in pools.iterrows()}
print("ACTIVITY RATES (cost per unit of driver)")
for _, p in pools.iterrows():
    print(f"  {p['cost_pool']:<16} ${rate_of[p['cost_pool']]:>10,.2f} per {p['driver_unit']}")

# Allocate to each model
prod['abc_oh'] = (prod['assembly_hours_per_unit'] * rate_of['assembly']
                  + prod['kwh_capacity']          * rate_of['battery_systems']
                  + prod['test_cycles_per_unit']  * rate_of['quality_testing']
                  + rate_of['logistics'] + rate_of['facilities'])
prod['abc_profit'] = prod['avg_price_usd'] - prod['direct_materials_per_unit'] - prod['abc_oh']
prod['abc_margin'] = prod['abc_profit'] / prod['avg_price_usd'] * 100

NoteResolution — who’s the profit engine?



The flashy per-car margins belong to S/X — but they’re a small slice in total (~9% between them). Model Y and Model 3 are ~86% of the profit in our simulated Fremont world — directionally right for the real Tesla, where the 3/Y are ~95% of volume. The humble volume cars carry the company; the premium cars are a high-margin garnish, and the Cybertruck earns far less than its sticker suggests. “Most profitable per car” and “where the money is” are different questions — the volume cars win mostly on sheer volume, and ABC then sharpens the picture, deflating the premium cars’ apparent margins.

section: The trap: should Tesla drop the Cybertruck?
text:
The trap: should Tesla drop the Cybertruck?






NoteDiscussion



Cybertruck looks weakest under ABC — suppose Tesla drops it. Which of the $9.2 bn of pools actually disappear? Go pool by pool — assembly lines, battery plant, test labs, logistics, the building — and bring back a number.


Debrief, then run the check:

cyber = prod[prod['model'] == 'Cybertruck'].iloc[0]
cyber_oh_annual = cyber['abc_oh'] * cyber['annual_volume_fremont'] / 1e6
others_vol = prod.loc[prod['model'] != 'Cybertruck', 'annual_volume_fremont'].sum()
print("DISCONTINUATION CHECK — Cybertruck")
print(f"  Weakest margin under ABC:           {cyber['abc_margin']:.0f}%")
print(f"  Overhead ABC allocates to it:       ${cyber_oh_annual:,.0f} m/yr")
print(f"  Worst-case reload onto survivors:   +${cyber_oh_annual*1e6/others_vol:,.0f} per car")

DISCONTINUATION CHECK — Cybertruck
  Weakest margin under ABC:           41%
  Overhead ABC allocates to it:       $485 m/yr
  Worst-case reload onto survivors:   +$407 per car


But allocated ≠ avoidable. Most of the $9.2 bn is shared, committed capacity — the building, the assembly lines, the battery plant — it stays whether or not Cybertruck exists. Worst case (assume none of it is avoidable): the full pot must now be carried by fewer cars — $485m ÷ 1,190,000 survivors ≈ +$407 each — and now another model looks weak…






WarningThe death spiral



Drop a product because allocated cost makes it look weak → its overhead reloads onto the survivors → now another looks weak → drop that → … until nothing is “profitable.” The error: allocated cost ≠ avoidable cost. Only costs that genuinely disappear matter for a drop decision — which is exactly Session 4.

title: Session 3 — Cost Allocation & ABC
text:
Key takeaways






NoteKey takeaways




How you allocate shared overhead decides which product looks profitable. A single volume rate causes cross-subsidisation.
ABC charges each cost pool by the driver that causes it; respecting the cost hierarchy (unit/batch/product/facility) is why complex low-volume products are under-costed by volume allocation.
ABC changes the distribution of profit, not the total — but the distribution is the decision-relevant part. Model Y + Model 3 are ~86% of the profit in our simulated Fremont world — directionally right for the real Tesla, where the 3/Y are ~95% of volume.
Allocated cost ≠ avoidable cost. Dropping a product on allocated cost invites the death spiral (→ Session 4).
Absorption costing is mandatory for external reports (IAS 2) — and because it parks fixed overhead in inventory, overproduction can inflate reported profit: legal, real, value-destroying, and self-reversing when the units finally sell. Managers watch variable costing alongside it.









NoteTesla case — Part C



Part C — “Wednesday: one factory, five models, one pot of overhead” of the week-long Tesla case, Five Days at Fremont (also on Moodle) — read during the ABC hands-on. Seven questions, in order: C1 (the plant-wide rate), C2 (two ABC rates by calculator), C3 (the Cybertruck column), C4 (where the money lives — and the drop-the-Cybertruck trap), ▸ C5 (the absorption-costing discovery), C6 (auditing the $9,200m pot), C7 (round two of the death spiral). The session ran out of clock before the group work, so every solution is written out in full below, with the common slips named. Work each question with a calculator first, then open it.








NotePart C — full solutions, C1 to C7





C1 — the plant-wide rate. One pot, one volume, one rate: $9,200m ÷ 1,230,000 cars = $7,480 per car — every model carries the same. Model 3: 39,000 − 15,000 − 7,480 = $16,520 a car (margin ≈ 42%). Model X: 99,000 − 32,000 − 7,480 = $59,520 a car (margin ≈ 60%). “Pour the factory into premium,” surely — the verdict C4 unravels. Common slip: taking margin on cost (16,520 ÷ 22,480 = 73%) instead of on price.
C2 — two ABC rates by calculator. One pool, one causal driver, one division — exactly how the exam asks it. Battery systems: $3,200m ÷ 87.67m kWh = $36.50 per kWh. Assembly: $2,400m ÷ 14.56m hours = $164.84 per hour. Units in millions on both sides. $3,200,000,000 ÷ 87.67 gives “$36.5m per kWh” — the sanity check catches it: a 75 kWh pack at $36.50 carries ≈ $2,700 of battery-plant overhead, which is plausible; $2.7bn a car is not. Where the driver totals come from: hours = Σ(volume × hrs per car) = 14.56m; kWh = Σ(volume × kWh per car) = 87.67m.

Profit per car: 80,000 − 35,000 − 12,121 = $32,879 → margin 41%, against 47% under the volume rate. Annual ≈ $1.3bn, ≈ 5% of the total. The paragraph: the $4,641 gap (12,121 − 7,480) was being paid by the simple, high-volume cars — cross-subsidisation. Batch- and product-level activity was spread as though it were unit-level — the cost hierarchy names why. The usual slip: dropping the two per-vehicle pools ($2,276.42) gives ≈ $9,844 — the margin falls, but the sign never flips. Rounding: the $/car cells use unrounded rates; cross-multiplying the printed rounded rates gives the same ≈ $12,121. The line to keep: ABC did not change total overhead by a dollar — it changed who carries it. Complexity, not just volume, drives the pot.
C4 — where the money lives, and the reply. Profit = per-car margin × volume. A Model X’s $56,749 × 20,000 ≈ $1.1bn; a Model Y’s $18,391 × 650,000 ≈ $12.0bn → Model Y + Model 3 ≈ 86% of the ≈ $24.1bn total. Both sentences hold; they answer different questions.

“The ≈ $485m is what ABC allocates to the Cybertruck, not what we would save — pool by pool, almost none of it dies with the model: the building stays, the battery plant’s capacity is committed, the lines and labs are shared; only some logistics genuinely goes. Worst case the full ≈ $485m re-spreads over the 1,190,000 surviving cars at ≈ +$407 each, and that road ends in the death spiral. Since Model Y + Model 3 already carry ≈ 86% of the profit, the question isn’t the Cybertruck’s margin — it’s which costs would actually disappear, and nothing we computed today answers that.”

Why that scores full marks: allocated ≠ avoidable, argued pool by pool · the reload spread over the survivors, not the 40,000 · the endgame named. Pool by pool, if you want the figures: facilities ≈ $52m (the building stays) · battery ≈ $180m (capacity committed) · assembly ≈ $165m (shared lines) · testing ≈ $49m (largely shared) · logistics ≈ $39m (the most genuinely avoidable). Slips: treating allocated overhead as a cash saving; and “so Model X matters most” — the per-car and total rankings are different orderings.
▸ C5 — the absorption trick. Sales fixed at 120,000; the bonus rides on absorption-costing profit (fixed overhead baked into each car’s cost). Produce 120,000: fixed overhead per car = $1,200m ÷ 120,000 = $10,000 → (45,000 − 30,000 − 10,000) × 120,000 = $600m. Variable costing — fixed overhead expensed in full each period, never parked in a unit — agrees: $600m. Produce 150,000, sell 120,000: the pot spreads thinner, $1,200m ÷ 150,000 = $8,000 a car → (45,000 − 30,000 − 8,000) × 120,000 = $840m. Variable costing still says $600m. The missing $240m = 30,000 unsold cars × $8,000, parked in inventory — “the cost waits”, weaponised. Name it: earnings management through overproduction (Roychowdhury 2006, JAE) — a real-activities manipulation: legal (absorption is what external reporting requires), value-destroying (cash tied up in unsold metal, write-down risk), and self-reversing when the cars finally sell. Slips: computing the produce-150,000 profit on 150,000 sold (demand is fixed at 120,000); claiming variable-costing profit also rises; saying the $240m “disappeared” — it sits in inventory and hits COGS when the cars sell, or worse, as a write-down. The line everyone leaves with: producing more than you sell can flatter reported profit — which is why managers also watch variable costing, where the trick does not work.
C6 — audit the pot. Exhibit C-4’s working list totals $12,000m; the pot we used all day was $9,200m. Three lines do not belong, for three different reasons:

Head-office administration + national advertising ($1,900m) — a period cost (SG&A): it sits below gross profit and is caused by no car.
Paint-shop retooling, completed last year ($600m) — sunk: a past cost never enters this period’s production overhead.
Battery-plant electricity ($300m) — a double-count: metered separately, but already inside the $3,200m battery pool.

12,000 − 1,900 − 600 − 300 = $9,200m, and the $7,480 rate is unchanged. An allocation can be wrong before you pick a single driver — audit the numerator first. Slips: striking Facilities on “the building isn’t caused by any car” — facility-level cost is production overhead, the hierarchy’s bottom row; keeping the $1,900m because “advertising helps sell cars”; adding the $300m to the battery pool instead of recognising it is already inside.
C7 — run the rule a second time. The CFO drops the Cybertruck anyway. Worst case nothing is saved, so the dead model’s share re-spreads: ≈ $485m ÷ 1,190,000 survivors ≈ +$407 onto every survivor’s ABC overhead.

text:
Accounting: the information system of a business
Accounting is how an organisation measures, records, summarises and communicates its economic activity. Without it, managers fly blind — you can’t manage what you can’t measure. And it is costly — systems, people, time. It survives for one reason: the decisions it improves are worth more than it costs. Much of it, in fact, exists for life inside the firm — costing, budgets, standard costs as internal “prices” — rather than for outside investors (Ball 2026, Journal of Accounting and Economics).

The foundation: A = L + E
Before management accounting, one equation underlies all accounting. Everything a business controls (its assets) was funded either by borrowing (liabilities) or by its owners (equity):
\[\text{Assets} = \text{Liabilities} + \text{Equity}\]
It always balances — every pound of resource came from somewhere. Watch it stay balanced as you start a small business:






NotePredict (show of hands)



Step 3 below spends £2,000 of the business’s cash on an espresso machine. Before we run the cell — show of hands: does the equation still balance? And which side moves?



steps = pd.DataFrame([
    ["Put in £5,000 of your own cash",        5000,    0, 5000, "cash 5,000"],
    ["...and borrow £3,000 from the bank",    8000, 3000, 5000, "cash 8,000"],
    ["Buy a £2,000 espresso machine",         8000, 3000, 5000, "cash 6,000 + machine 2,000"],
], columns=["Event", "Assets (£)", "Liabilities (£)", "Equity (£)", "What the assets are"])
steps["Balances? A = L + E"] = steps["Assets (£)"] == steps["Liabilities (£)"] + steps["Equity (£)"]
print(steps.to_string(index=False))

                             Event  Assets (£)  Liabilities (£)  Equity (£)        What the assets are  Balances? A = L + E
    Put in £5,000 of your own cash        5000                0        5000                 cash 5,000                 True
...and borrow £3,000 from the bank        8000             3000        5000                 cash 8,000                 True
     Buy a £2,000 espresso machine        8000             3000        5000 cash 6,000 + machine 2,000                 True


Buying the machine just swaps one asset (cash) for another (equipment) — total assets, and the equation, don’t move.






Note▸ The machinery underneath: T-accounts (a first look)





How do accountants record those three events so the equation can never break? Every account gets a T: one side for increases, the other for decreases. By centuries-old convention, assets grow on the left (a “debit”, Dr) and liabilities and equity grow on the right (a “credit”, Cr) — and every transaction posts equal amounts left and right, always touching at least two accounts. That is double-entry bookkeeping, and it is why A = L + E always balances: every entry adds the same amount to both sides of the network, so the equation can’t break.
Our espresso start-up again — events (1) £5,000 own cash, (2) £3,000 loan, (3) £2,000 machine:
       CASH (asset)          EQUIPMENT (asset)      BANK LOAN (liability)     OWNER'S EQUITY
      Dr    │    Cr            Dr    │    Cr           Dr    │    Cr           Dr    │    Cr
  (1) 5,000 │              (3) 2,000 │                       │ (2) 3,000             │ (1) 5,000
  (2) 3,000 │ (3) 2,000              │                       │                       │
  ──────────┼──────────    ──────────┼──────────      ───────┼──────────      ───────┼──────────
  bal 6,000 │              bal 2,000 │                       │ bal 3,000             │ bal 5,000
Check: assets £6,000 + £2,000 = £8,000; liabilities £3,000 + equity £5,000 = £8,000 — the balance is built in, transaction by transaction.
That’s as deep as this course goes — we use the numbers rather than book them. But when Session 3 shows a cost “moving into inventory”, this is the machinery doing it.









TipOne term to get straight: cost vs expense



A cost is a resource you give up to get something. It becomes an expense when it’s used up to earn revenue — sometimes straight away (today’s advertising), sometimes later: a machine turns into expense gradually as depreciation (spreading the machine’s cost over the years it helps earn revenue); a car’s build cost waits on the shelf as inventory and only becomes an expense — “cost of goods sold” — when the car is sold. So the same £ can be a cost (asset) now and an expense later — keep the two ideas distinct.











A cost becomes an expense when it’s used up — instantly (advertising), gradually (depreciation), or only when sold (inventory → cost of goods sold). Session 3 leans hard on that third lane.
The same firm keeps three sets of books — three views of the same reality for three audiences — financial (for outsiders), management (for insiders), and tax (for the authorities). Tesla’s shareholders read “FY2024 revenue $97.7bn, cost of revenues $80.2bn, operating income $7.1bn”; Tesla’s plant manager reads “shave 10% off battery-cell cost and we save ~$500 a car.” Both true; different jobs.

NoteDiscussion



Tesla wants to borrow $5bn from a bank; separately, a Tesla manager must decide the Model Y’s price. Which kind of accounting does each need — and why?


And here is why the internal kind matters so much — Herbert Simon’s thought experiment: a Martian points a telescope at Earth, with organisations showing up as green areas and market transactions as thin red lines. The Martian sees mostly green — it would never call this a “market economy”. Inside the green there are no market prices to guide decisions; what firms use instead is management accounting.






ImportantThis course is about the second one



Financial accounting is required by law. Management accounting is chosen by managers because it helps them run the business. It serves three jobs — planning (“what should we do?”), decisions (“which option is better?”), and control (“did we hit the plan?”) — and they map onto your week:

Accounting numbers help run a business in two different ways — and the course’s two halves split along that line. Part 1 (Dr Çetin) is about numbers that help you decide: what does a Model Y cost, should we cut its price, make the part or buy it. Part 2 (Dr Timmermans) is about numbers that help you steer people: targets, budgets, bonuses, performance evaluation. The formal names are decision-facilitating and decision-influencing (Demski & Feltham 1976) — and neither works alone: good numbers nobody acts on are wasted, and targets built on bad numbers backfire.






Note▸ Does management accounting actually matter? (the research)





Bloom, Eifert, Mahajan, McKenzie & Roberts (“Does Management Matter? Evidence from India”, QJE 2013) ran a randomised trial in Indian textile firms: those given better management practices (much of it basic management accounting — measuring, monitoring, target-setting) raised productivity by ~17%. The “soft” toolkit you’re learning has hard, causal effects on firm performance. (Notice the trial bundles both roles — measurement to facilitate decisions and target-setting to influence behaviour.)



Back to the CFO. The question is about cost — but the first thing a good analyst asks is: cost of what?

“Cost of what?” — the cost object
A cost object is anything you want the cost of: a product (Model Y), a department (the Fremont factory), a customer (a fleet buyer), a project (Cybertruck development). The same factory cost is “direct” to the factory but “indirect” to a single car — two terms we’ll define properly in a few minutes — so you must fix the cost object first.






WarningOne idea to carry all week



The “cost” of something depends on the question. The cost of a Model Y for financial reporting (an average) differs from its cost for pricing (incremental) and for make-or-buy (avoidable). Hold onto this — it returns every session.


We classify costs two ways, and each answers a different manager’s question.

text:
Classification 1 — by behaviour: how does profit move with volume?

Variable costs change in total as volume changes (battery cells: more cars, more cells).
Fixed costs stay the same in total across a sensible range of volume — accountants call this the relevant range (factory insurance: the same premium at 400k or 500k cars).









Figure 1: Variable, fixed and total cost — in total. Illustrative round numbers to show the shapes — not Tesla’s actuals; Session 2 estimates the real ones from Tesla’s quarterly data (Compustat).











Note▸ Outside the relevant range





The “fixed” label is only guaranteed inside the relevant range. Push volume far enough beyond it and fixed costs step up (a second assembly line, new premises) and variable costs bend (overtime, bottlenecks); fall far below it and each car costs far more to build — an underused plant, a crew still finding its rhythm on the line. The left panel’s fixed-cost steps land in total cost as jumps at both edges of the range, and the straight line’s intercept is not the true cost at zero volume — the low band runs on $2.4bn of fixed cost, not the extrapolated $3.0bn. Every fixed/variable call carries an implicit volume range — check it before you rely on it.








Figure 2: Outside the relevant range the linear model fails on both sides: fixed cost steps between capacity bands (left), and both steps land in total cost as jumps — $0.6bn at 200k, $0.8bn at 500k (right). Below the range the first cars cost far more each (the concave start-up bow), and the curve runs on the low band’s $2.4bn of fixed cost: the line’s $3.0bn intercept is not the true cost at zero volume. Illustrative numbers — the same $3bn / $20k per car inside the range as above.









The twist that trips everyone: per-unit behaviour
Flip to per car and the pattern inverts — and this is a classic beginner trap:

fixed = 3_000_000_000           # $3bn fixed — same illustrative number as the plot above, not Tesla's actual
for n in (300_000, 500_000):
    print(f"  At {n:,} cars: fixed cost per car = ${fixed/n:,.0f}")

  At 300,000 cars: fixed cost per car = $10,000
  At 500,000 cars: fixed cost per car = $6,000


Same $3bn — but “per car” it slid from $10,000 to $6,000. “Fixed cost per unit” is an artificial number: it depends on a volume you pick.






NoteYour turn (then check)



You’re the analyst. At 300,000 cars the accountants report a full unit cost of $30,000 per car ($20,000 variable + the $10,000 fixed-per-car figure we just computed). The CFO asks for the total cost budget at 500,000 cars. In pairs: compute it and commit to a number before we run the next cell.



budget_wrong = (fixed/300_000 + 20_000) * 500_000 / 1e9
budget_right = (20_000 * 500_000 + fixed) / 1e9
print(f"  Budget 500k cars using the 300k unit cost: ${budget_wrong:,.1f}bn  ← WRONG")
print(f"  Correct (variable per car + total fixed):   ${budget_right:,.1f}bn  ← think in TOTALS")

  Budget 500k cars using the 300k unit cost: $15.0bn  ← WRONG
  Correct (variable per car + total fixed):   $13.0bn  ← think in TOTALS


Where did the $30,000 come from? It was a correct total-cost build at 300,000 cars — $3.0bn fixed + $20,000 × 300,000 = $9.0bn; ÷ 300,000 = $30,000 a car. Correct arithmetic, frozen at one volume — the error is only in scaling it.
The trap: never budget by scaling a full unit cost (fixed cost baked in) to a new volume. A purely variable unit cost is fine to scale.








Figure 3: The trap, drawn: the frozen $10,000 figure understates fixed cost per car below 300k cars and overstates it above — at 500k the $4,000-a-car gap is the $2bn phantom in the budget.











ImportantMisconception check



“Fixed cost per unit” feels like a real per-car number you can add to variable cost and scale up. It isn’t — total fixed cost is flat; the per-unit figure is just that flat number divided by whatever volume you chose. For decisions, think in total costs, not unit costs. And two names worth keeping: a per-unit figure built by division is an average cost; the extra cost of one more car is its marginal cost. Session 2 leans on the first; Session 4 runs on the second.

Classification 2 — by traceability: what does this product cost?

Direct costs can be traced to the cost object economically (the battery pack in this Model Y).
Indirect costs (overhead) can’t be — they’re shared and must be allocated (the factory manager’s salary covers Y, 3, S and X). How to allocate is the whole of Session 3.









Figure 4: How a cost reaches one Model Y: direct costs are traced; overhead is allocated by a rule. The allocation arrow is the whole of Session 3.











Note▸ Why these distinctions run the modern economy





Software is the extreme cost structure: huge fixed cost to build, near-zero variable cost to serve one more user. De Ridder (2024, “Market Power and Innovation in the Intangible Economy”, American Economic Review 114(1), 199–251 — LSE Economics) shows that as intangibles spread, this cost structure alone can explain rising markups, fewer new challengers entering, and slower productivity growth. And because ever more cost is indirect — shared software, data, R&D — “what does this product cost?” keeps getting harder to answer. That question is Session 3.

NoteKey takeaways




Accounting measures, records and communicates economic activity; underneath it all, A = L + E always balances.

The high-low method
The simplest rule: take the period with the highest activity and the one with the lowest, and assume the cost difference between them is purely variable.
\[b\;(\text{variable cost per unit}) = \frac{\text{Cost}_{\text{high}} - \text{Cost}_{\text{low}}}{\text{Units}_{\text{high}} - \text{Units}_{\text{low}}}\qquad\qquad a\;(\text{fixed cost}) = \text{Cost}_{\text{high}} - b\times\text{Units}_{\text{high}}\]
We’ll learn it on a small, simple 12-month dataset for one product line (so the mechanics are obvious), then face Tesla’s real data after the break.

Key takeaways






NoteKey takeaways




In the real world the fixed/variable split is estimated, not given.
High-low uses two points — quick, fragile. Regression (OLS) uses all of them and tells you how well the line fits (R²) and whether to trust it (p-value). Same idea in Excel and Python.

A price cut survives only if the extra volume keeps you above break-even.

section: Sunk costs: the $6.2 bn goes in the bin
text:
Sunk costs: the $6.2 bn goes in the bin
A sunk cost is money already spent that you can’t get back. It fails gate 1, so by the rule it’s never relevant — no matter how big or how painful.

Gigafactory Nevada: Tesla reported $6.2bn invested by early 2023, with a $3.6bn expansion underway — real figures, from Tesla’s own reporting.
Make batteries there or buy from Panasonic — that money is gone either way → sunk. It must not touch the make-or-buy decision.
What can still matter is the factory’s resale value, or what else the space could earn — see opportunity cost, next.







NotePredict (show of hands)



Hypothetical scenario: Tesla has spent $200m developing a new battery design — and it doesn’t work. A competitor offers a working alternative for $150m. What should Tesla do?

keep trying — we’ve already spent $200m · (b) buy the alternative — the $200m is sunk · (c) keep trying — $200m > $150m · (d) negotiate to split the costs









ImportantMisconception check — the sunk-cost fallacy



Hands up for (a) or (c)? Both are the same error: the $200m is gone under every option, so it can’t help you choose. “We’ve spent so much, we can’t stop now” feels responsible; whether you’ve sunk $5 or $6bn changes nothing about which choice is best from here. The same instinct at human scale: finishing a terrible film because you’re an hour in; eating past full because you paid. The textbook demonstration — Arkes & Blumer (1985): theatre-goers randomly given a discounted season ticket went to fewer plays than those who paid full price — the more people had sunk, the more they showed up to “not waste” it. Economists’ nickname for the error is the Concorde fallacy — the British and French governments kept funding a supersonic jet everyone knew would never pay back; a monument to sunk-cost thinking at Mach 2. Future-and-differs only.

title: Session 4 — Decision Making & Relevant Costs
section: Opportunity costs: the invisible cost that is relevant
text:
Opportunity costs: the invisible cost that is relevant
An opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up. It’s future, and it differs between options — so it’s relevant — but there’s no invoice for it, so it’s the cost managers most often miss.

If Tesla uses the Gigafactory floor to build batteries, it can’t use that floor for Megapacks — Tesla’s grid-scale battery-storage product, sold to utilities: ~3.9 MWh a unit, a battery the size of a shipping container. The Megapack profit it forgoes is a real cost of making batteries — even though no one writes it down.

The pattern to remember: sunk costs are visible but irrelevant; opportunity costs are invisible but relevant. We weight them exactly backwards by instinct.








Figure 2: Visibility and relevance are different axes — and the two costs that trip managers up sit in opposite corners.

make_var = b.loc['total_variable', 'in_house_per_kwh']      # $/kWh incremental in-house
buy_var  = b.loc['total_variable', 'panasonic_per_kwh']     # $/kWh from Panasonic, landed
buy_quote = b.loc['purchase_price', 'panasonic_per_kwh']    # Panasonic's quoted price
buy_ship  = b.loc['logistics', 'panasonic_per_kwh']         # transport & handling
make_fix = b.loc['annual_fixed_cost_millions', 'in_house_per_kwh']   # $m/yr existing fixed

prod = pd.read_csv('../../data/simulated/product_activity_drivers.csv')
demand_kwh = (prod['annual_volume_fremont'] * prod['kwh_capacity']).sum()

print(f"In-house variable cost    : ${make_var:.0f} / kWh")
print(f"Buy from Panasonic, landed: ${buy_var:.0f} / kWh  (= ${buy_quote:.0f} price + ${buy_ship:.0f} logistics)")
print(f"In-house existing fixed   : ${make_fix:,.0f} m / year")
print(f"Tesla's battery demand    : {demand_kwh/1e6:.1f} m kWh / year")
print(f"\nNaive 'full cost' in-house = {make_var:.0f} + {make_fix:,.0f}m/{demand_kwh/1e6:.1f}m "
      f"= ${make_var + make_fix*1e6/demand_kwh:.0f}/kWh  vs buy ${buy_var:.0f}/kWh")

In-house variable cost    : $70 / kWh
Buy from Panasonic, landed: $90 / kWh  (= $85 price + $5 logistics)
In-house existing fixed   : $800 m / year
Tesla's battery demand    : 87.7 m kWh / year

Naive 'full cost' in-house = 70 + 800m/87.7m = $79/kWh  vs buy $90/kWh


Scope note: these are battery-cell costs (simulated data). Industry headlines usually quote pack-level prices (~$115–140/kWh, BloombergNEF 2024), which add pack assembly, housing and battery management on top of the cell — a different scope, so don’t compare the two.
So far in-house even looks cheaper on full cost. But the real decision is usually “should we make the next batch in-house, or buy it?” — and for that, the existing $800m fixed cost is irrelevant — it’s there whichever way you choose, so it fails the “differs” test (the truly sunk cost is the ~$6.2bn build):

saving = buy_var - make_var
new_line_fixed = 400          # $m/yr for a NEW line (illustrative)
be_kwh = new_line_fixed * 1e6 / saving
print(f"EXISTING line : make ${make_var:.0f} vs buy ${buy_var:.0f}/kWh  →  making saves ${saving:.0f}/kWh")
print(f"NEW ${new_line_fixed}m/yr line: break-even = ${new_line_fixed}m / ${saving:.0f} = {be_kwh/1e6:.0f}m kWh of extra demand")

EXISTING line : make $70 vs buy $90/kWh  →  making saves $20/kWh
NEW $400m/yr line: break-even = $400m / $20 = 20m kWh of extra demand


On the existing line the fixed cost is unchanged either way, so only the variable costs compare; a new line’s fixed cost does differ — hence the break-even:

extra = np.linspace(0, 40, 200)                       # extra demand, m kWh/yr
cost_buy  = buy_var * extra                           # $m/yr: variable only
cost_make = new_line_fixed + make_var * extra         # $m/yr: new fixed + variable

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
ax.plot(extra, cost_buy, color=BLUE, lw=2, label=f'BUY the extra (\\${buy_var:.0f}/kWh, no new fixed)')
ax.plot(extra, cost_make, color=TESLA_RED, lw=2, label=f'MAKE on a new line (\\${new_line_fixed}m fixed + \\${make_var:.0f}/kWh)')
ax.axvline(be_kwh/1e6, color='0.5', ls='--', lw=1)
ax.annotate(f'break-even ≈ {be_kwh/1e6:.0f}m kWh', xy=(be_kwh/1e6, buy_var*be_kwh/1e6),
            xytext=(23, 1150), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='0.4'))
ax.text(7, 120, 'buy cheaper here', color=BLUE, fontsize=10)
ax.text(27, 120, 'make cheaper here', color=TESLA_RED, fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlabel('extra battery demand (m kWh / year)')
ax.set_ylabel('total cost of the extra ($m / year)')
ax.legend(loc='upper left'); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 3: Illustrative: a new $400m/yr line pays for itself only beyond ~20m kWh of extra demand — below that, buy the extra batteries.











NoteDiscussion



Put yourself in the CFO’s chair. So far the $800m has been irrelevant — it’s there whichever way the next batch goes. Now the board asks a bigger question: should Tesla be in the battery business at all, or outsource everything and clear the floor? Does the $800m still fail the “differs” test? And what happens to the floor?



The twist: the same cost, a different question
For the marginal batch above, the $800m was irrelevant — it didn’t differ. But note what that $800m is: ongoing cash operating cost — utilities, maintenance, salaried staff, leases — not depreciation of the sunk ~$6.2bn build (that stays sunk forever). Now take the strategic question you just debated: should Tesla be in the battery business at all, or outsource entirely and repurpose the Gigafactory? For that decision the $800m of ongoing cash cost now differs — closing the line avoids it, so it becomes relevant — and the freed floor could earn ~$1.1bn/year in Megapack contribution (profit forgone, not revenue). Same dollars, different relevance, because the decision changed:

megapack_opp = 1_100         # $m/yr Megapack CONTRIBUTION forgone if floor stays in batteries (illustrative)
make_total = make_var * demand_kwh / 1e6 + make_fix          # variable + now-AVOIDABLE factory fixed
buy_total  = buy_var  * demand_kwh / 1e6                     # pure variable (factory closed)
print(f"{'':30}{'MAKE':>12}{'BUY':>12}")
print(f"{'Variable battery cost ($m)':30}{make_var*demand_kwh/1e6:>12,.0f}{buy_total:>12,.0f}")
print(f"{'Factory fixed — now avoidable':30}{make_fix:>12,.0f}{0:>12,.0f}")
print(f"{'Opportunity cost (Megapacks)':30}{megapack_opp:>12,.0f}{0:>12,.0f}")
print(f"{'= relevant total ($m)':30}{make_total+megapack_opp:>12,.0f}{buy_total:>12,.0f}")
winner = 'MAKE' if make_total + megapack_opp < buy_total else 'BUY'
print(f"\nRelevant totals: MAKE ${make_total+megapack_opp:,.0f}m vs BUY ${buy_total:,.0f}m  →  {winner}")

                                      MAKE         BUY
Variable battery cost ($m)           6,137       7,890
Factory fixed — now avoidable          800           0
Opportunity cost (Megapacks)         1,100           0
= relevant total ($m)                8,037       7,890

Relevant totals: MAKE $8,037m vs BUY $7,890m  →  BUY


Counting the avoidable factory cost and the forgone Megapack profit, the answer flips.






ImportantThe real-world answer: do both



Tesla makes 4680 cells in-house and buys from Panasonic, LG and CATL. The numbers rarely settle it alone — qualitative factors decide the margin: supply security (don’t depend on one supplier), keeping battery tech proprietary, flexibility to scale. Relevant-cost analysis narrows the choice; judgement finishes it.
The supply-security factor has a front page: in May 2017 a shortage of Bosch steering systems meant thousands of BMWs could not be built — BMW car production disrupted due to supply problems (FT, 29 May 2017). Dependence on a single supplier is a cost that appears in no relevant-cost table until it lands all at once.

Hypothetical scenario: a rental company offers to buy 50,000 Model 3 at $30,000 — below the $39,000 list. Accept?






NoteThe cost card



Illustrative, simplified Model 3 costs: variable cost $25,000/car; allocated fixed overhead $8,000/car → “full cost” $33,000.

Commit before the maths: accept or reject? And what’s the minimum price per car you’d take? Show of hands when time’s up — then hold your answer to one more question: what would change your mind?








NoteReveal

variable, alloc_fixed = 25_000, 8_000
full = variable + alloc_fixed

print("FULL-COST VIEW (the trap):")
print(f"  offer ${offer:,} − full cost ${full:,} = ${offer-full:+,}/car  →  'reject!'\n")
print("RELEVANT-COST VIEW (spare capacity):")
print(f"  offer ${offer:,} − variable ${variable:,} = ${offer-variable:+,}/car contribution")

  offer $30,000 − full cost $33,000 = $-3,000/car  →  'reject!'

RELEVANT-COST VIEW (spare capacity):
  offer $30,000 − variable $25,000 = $+5,000/car contribution
  × 50,000 cars = $+250 m  →  ACCEPT (with spare capacity)


The $8,000 allocated fixed overhead is there with or without this order — it is not caused by the order, so it fails “differs”.

ax[0].bar(['Offer', 'Variable', 'Fixed\n(allocated)'], [offer/1000, -variable/1000, -alloc_fixed/1000],
          color=[GREEN, TESLA_RED, '#b08']); ax[0].axhline(0, color='k', lw=.6)

          color=[GREEN, TESLA_RED, GREEN]); ax[1].axhline(0, color='k', lw=.6)
ax[1].set_title(f'Relevant cost: {offer-variable:+,} / car  → accept')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()







Figure 4: Full cost says reject; relevant cost says accept — the fixed overhead is there either way.









The hinge: spare capacity
At full capacity, every special car displaces a normal $39,000 sale — and that displaced sale’s contribution is an opportunity cost:

reg_cm = list_price - variable        # contribution given up if a normal sale is displaced
print(f"Opportunity cost = displaced contribution = ${reg_cm:,}/car")
print(f"Special contribution ${offer-variable:,} < ${reg_cm:,}  →  REJECT at full capacity")

Opportunity cost = displaced contribution = $14,000/car
Special contribution $5,000 < $14,000  →  REJECT at full capacity


The rule: with spare capacity, accept if price > variable cost; at full capacity, accept only if the special contribution beats the displaced contribution.






ImportantMisconception check



Both traps are the same mistake: letting a fixed/allocated cost (unchanged by this decision) drive a choice it doesn’t actually change. Strip to what’s future and differs — then, separately, ask whether capacity turns spare resources into an opportunity cost.

Machine capacity is 220 hours (13,200 minutes); a strike has cut assembly labour to 500 hours (30,000 minutes). With the machine as the only worry, the ranking rule puts Touring first (£12 vs £7.50 per machine-minute). But now both constraints bind at once — rank by which? Neither: with several scarce resources, ranking gives an answer, not the best answer. Let a search do the work — Excel’s Solver (the companion’s “Product mix — Solver” tab walks it through), or one line of Python:

from scipy.optimize import linprog
# max 15M + 12T  s.t.  labour 3M+3T ≤ 30,000 · machine 2M+T ≤ 13,200 · M ≤ 4,000 · T ≤ 7,000
res = linprog(c=[-15, -12], A_ub=[[3, 3], [2, 1]], b_ub=[30_000, 13_200],
              bounds=[(0, 4_000), (0, 7_000)], method='highs')
m_opt, t_opt = res.x

rk_t = 7_000; rk_m = min(4_000, (30_000 - 3*rk_t)//3, (13_200 - rk_t)//2)   # rank by machine-minute
rl_m = 4_000; rl_t = min(7_000, (30_000 - 3*rl_m)//3, 13_200 - 2*rl_m)      # rank by labour-minute
print(f"Optimal mix : {m_opt:,.0f} Mountain + {t_opt:,.0f} Touring  →  £{-res.fun:,.0f}")
print(f"Rank by machine-minute (Touring first): £{12*rk_t + 15*rk_m:,.0f}")
print(f"Rank by labour-minute (Mountain first) : £{15*rl_m + 12*rl_t:,.0f}")

Optimal mix : 3,200 Mountain + 6,800 Touring  →  £129,600
Rank by machine-minute (Touring first): £129,000
Rank by labour-minute (Mountain first) : £122,400


At the optimum both constraints are exactly used up — the answer sits where the two limits cross, which no single-constraint ranking can find. One scarce resource → rank by contribution per unit of it. Several → optimise (Solver, linprog). Same data, same answer, either tool.

title: Session 4 — Decision Making & Relevant Costs
text:
Key takeaways






NoteKey takeaways




A cost is relevant only if it’s future and differs between the options. Everything else is noise.
Sunk costs (visible, large) are irrelevant; opportunity costs (invisible) are relevant — we instinctively weight them backwards.
Keep-or-drop: compare the contribution you lose with the costs that actually disappear — allocated lines that survive never count (the death spiral’s antidote).
Make-or-buy: compare incremental costs; existing fixed cost doesn’t differ — only new fixed cost and opportunity cost count, and opportunity cost can flip the answer.
Special orders: accept if price > variable cost with spare capacity; at full capacity, the displaced contribution is an opportunity cost.
Constrained resource: rank by contribution per unit of the bottleneck — and with several constraints, optimise instead.

Every number today passed the same test before it counted: future, and different. Tomorrow the future arrives — the quarter closes, the flash numbers land, and Tesla misses the plan. Was it the market, or the factory? Price, volume, or efficiency — and whose fault? That’s variance analysis.
